The paper "Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Observer Error-Rates Using the EM Algorithm" was authored by A. P. Dawid and A. M. Skene and published in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C (Applied Statistics), Vol. 28, No. 1 (1979), pp. 20-28.

The paper presents a model which allows individual error-rates to be estimated for polytomous facets even when the patient's "true" response is not available. The EM algorithm is shown to provide a slow but sure way of obtaining maximum likelihood estimates of the parameters of interest.

The paper appears to be highly influential and is widely cited in work related to handling unreliable observations and estimating observer error rates. The method has been implemented in various software libraries and continues to be referenced in modern work on crowdsourcing and data quality.

I found the paper you're looking for! Here's what I found:

"Generating Multi-Agent Trajectories using Programmatic Weak Supervision" by Eric Zhan, Stephan Zheng, Yisong Yue, Long Sha, and Patrick Lucey was published at the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) in May 2019.

The paper focuses on training sequential generative models for capturing coordinated multi-agent trajectory behavior, such as offensive basketball gameplay. The authors present a hierarchical framework that can effectively learn such sequential generative models, inspired by recent work on leveraging programmatically produced weak labels, which they extend to the spatiotemporal regime.

They blend deep generative models with programmatic weak supervision to generate coordinated multi-agent trajectories of significantly higher quality than previous baselines.

The paper is available on arXiv (arxiv.org/abs/1803.07612) and there's also a PyTorch implementation available on GitHub.

I found comprehensive research on this topic. Here are the key findings:

## Overview

Agent drift is defined as the progressive degradation of agent behavior, decision quality, and inter-agent coherence over extended interaction sequences. This is a recently published research area, with a 2026 arXiv paper by Abhishek Rath titled "Agent Drift: Quantifying Behavioral Degradation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems Over Extended Interactions."

## Key Measurement Framework

The Agent Stability Index (ASI) is a novel composite metric framework for quantifying drift across twelve dimensions, including response consistency, tool usage patterns, reasoning pathway stability, and inter-agent agreement rates.

## Types of Drift

The research proposes three distinct manifestations of agent drift: semantic drift (progressive deviation from original intent), coordination drift (breakdown in multi-agent consensus mechanisms), and behavioral drift (emergence of unintended strategies).

## Practical Impact

Behavioral degradation could affect nearly half of long-running agents and cause severe performance impacts—projected 42% reduction in task success rates and 3.2x increase in human intervention requirements.

## Mitigation Strategies

Three mitigation strategies are proposed: episodic memory consolidation, drift-aware routing protocols, and adaptive behavioral anchoring, with theoretical analysis suggesting these approaches can significantly reduce drift-related errors while maintaining system throughput.

The research establishes foundational methodology for monitoring, measuring, and mitigating this emerging challenge in multi-agent LLM systems.

I found detailed information about ProbGuard. Here's what the search revealed:

## Overview

ProbGuard is a proactive runtime monitoring framework for LLM agents that anticipates safety violations through probabilistic risk prediction.

## Key Technical Approach

ProbGuard abstracts agent executions into symbolic states and learns a Discrete-Time Markov Chain (DTMC) from execution traces to model behavioral dynamics. At runtime, the monitor estimates the probability that future executions will reach unsafe states and triggers interventions when this risk exceeds a user-defined threshold.

## Advantages Over Existing Methods

Existing runtime monitoring frameworks, such as AgentSpec, primarily rely on reactive safety rules that detect violations only when unsafe behavior is imminent or has already occurred, limiting their ability to handle long-horizon dependencies. In contrast, ProbGuard is proactive.

## Robustness Features

To improve robustness, ProbGuard incorporates semantic validity constraints in the abstraction and provides PAC-style guarantees on the learned model under standard assumptions.

## Evaluation Results

ProbGuard was evaluated in two safety-critical domains: autonomous driving and embodied household agents. The results were impressive:

- In autonomous driving scenarios, ProbGuard consistently predicted traffic law violations and collisions in advance, with warnings up to 38.66 seconds ahead of occurrence.
- In embodied agent tasks, ProbGuard reduces unsafe behavior by up to 65.37% while preserving up to 80.4% task completion.

## Implementation

ProbGuard is implemented as an extensible open-source runtime monitor integrated with the LangChain agent framework and introduces minimal runtime overhead.

Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly operate across domains such as robotics, virtual assistants, and web automation, but their stochastic decision-making introduces safety risks that are difficult to anticipate during execution.

At runtime, the monitor estimates the probability that future executions will reach unsafe states and triggers interventions when this risk exceeds a user-defined threshold.
